To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the soil properties bulk density and water saturation can be used to predict the strength of solute transport at the field scale.

(1) the degree of water content and bulk density are important soil properties for predicting preferential transport in agricultural fields, and that (2) it should be possible, but not trivial, to upscale solute transport properties established at the column scale to the field scale.

preferential transport is the dominating transport process in cultivated topsoil under a steady-state flow regime and that preferential transport can be quantified by soil properties such as bulk density or soil water content. [2]
In summary, our research is concerned with

the quantification of the spatial heterogeneity in soil properties, hydrological state variables, and BTCs at the field scale and with its implications for the upscaling of solute transport models. [2]
the development of a conceptual framework for the estimation of solute transport at the field scale based on the spatial distribution of soil properties and hydrologic state variables. [2]
the development of a new method for upscaling solute transport at the field scale and larger.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spatial patterns in solute transport at the field scale are related with spatial patterns in soil properties.
the strength of preferential solute transport is related to the water saturation and the bulk density. [2]

the soil properties bulk density and soil water saturation can be used to predict the strength of preferential solute transport in a field with a high degree of confidence, but that the estimation approach has to be upscaled to the field scale.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
soil heterogeneities are important at all scales.

soil properties and hydrologic state variables can be used as predictors of the BTC shapes and the degree of preferential transport at the field scale, but that this is not the case at smaller spatial scales. [2]
solute transport at the field scale can be predicted with reasonable accuracy from a small number of soil properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the field-scale solute transport properties can be estimated from the soil properties, but that the estimation approaches need to be upscaled.
